lesson.title: The Long Tail on the Low End: Understanding Left Skew
lesson.summary: A left-skewed distribution has a longer tail stretching toward low values, which drags the mean below the median and signals that a few unusually small observations are influencing the average.
lesson.body:
When statisticians describe a distribution as skewed left, they are describing the tail, the thin stretched out part of the graph, not the location of the hump where most of the data piles up. In a left-skewed distribution, that thin tail stretches out toward the smaller values on the left side of the number line, while the bulk of the data, the tall part of the histogram, sits over toward the right. A useful way to remember the naming convention is that the tail points in the direction of the skew's name, so "skewed left" always means the tail, not the peak, is on the left.

Left skew has a direct and predictable effect on how the mean and median compare, and understanding why connects directly to what you already know about how each measure behaves. The median only cares about the position of values once they are sorted, so a few extremely small observations sitting far out in the left tail barely move it, they are still just the smallest few values in the list. The mean, by contrast, uses the actual numeric value of every observation, so those same extremely small numbers drag the arithmetic average down substantially. The result is a reliable pattern: in a left-skewed distribution, the mean is smaller than the median.

Here is a concrete case. Six students take a difficult final exam and score 95, 92, 90, 88, 85, and 40, where one student had a very bad day. Sorted in order: 40, 85, 88, 90, 92, 95. With six values, the median is the average of the third and fourth, which are 88 and 90, giving a median of 89. The mean is the sum divided by six: 40 + 85 + 88 + 90 + 92 + 95 = 490, and 490 divided by 6 is about 81.67. The mean, 81.67, sits noticeably below the median, 89, exactly the signature of left skew, because the single low score of 40 pulled the average down while barely nudging the median.

Left-skewed data shows up whenever most cases cluster near a natural ceiling with occasional cases falling well short of it. Age at death in a population with modern healthcare is a classic example: most people live into their seventies, eighties, or beyond, but a smaller number die much younger, stretching a tail toward zero. Scores on an easy exam where nearly everyone does well except for a handful of unprepared students follow the same pattern.

This shape also has a recognizable signature on other common graphs. On a boxplot, left skew typically shows up as a longer whisker, and any flagged outliers, stretching out on the low end, while the box itself, which represents the middle 50 percent of the data, sits closer to the high side of the display. Learning to recognize this pattern on a boxplot is just as important as recognizing it on a histogram, since boxplots are often the only graph provided on an exam question.

It is worth distinguishing genuine skew from a single unusual point. A distribution is called skewed when there is a consistent, gradually thinning tail made up of several observations, not just one isolated extreme value. When only one point sits far from the rest of the data, it may instead be best described as an outlier, a concept covered later in this unit, and the two ideas often appear together in the same data set.
